entries.meaning: Asks for the identity of a thing, an event, or an action, out of an open field of possibilities.
examples: What happened to the second box of files?
What did she say when you told her the price?
What are you looking at?
He asked me what I wanted for my birthday.
What was your father before he retired, a machinist?
What does the whole thing cost with tax and delivery?
What's in the trunk? Nothing that won't fit in the hall closet.
Nobody could tell us what the delay was about.

senses.head: Things, events, and actions
body: The default use: What happened?, What do you want?, What's in the bag? The answer can be anything at all, which is what separates it from which.

senses.head: A person's role or category
body: What is she? asks for an occupation, a nationality, a category — not a name. Beside it, Who is she? asks for the identity.

senses.head: Amount, price, and measure
body: What did it cost?, What does the whole thing weigh? Here what is doing the work of how much.

senses.head: Standing for a whole clause
body: What happened next? and What's going on? take an entire event as the answer, not a noun.

senses.head: As a request for repetition
body: Bare What? means "say that again", and in American English it is blunt — Sorry?, Excuse me?, and I'm sorry, what? are the polite versions, Huh? the casual one. For the incredulous You did what?, see what (echo).
examples: What happened to the second box of files?
What did she say when you told her the price?
What are you looking at?
He asked me what I wanted for my birthday.
What was your father before he retired, a machinist?
What does the whole thing cost with tax and delivery?
What's in the trunk? Nothing that won't fit in the hall closet.
Nobody could tell us what the delay was about.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /wət/ whenever it is not the accented word (I know what I want → [wət]); the t flaps into a following vowel, so what if is [wʌˈɾɪf] and what are you runs together as whaddaya; plain /w/ for most Americans, /hwʌt/ for speakers who keep the older onset
entries.русский: что — спрашивает о предмете, событии или действии из открытого, не заданного круга
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.type: interrogative pronoun (also a fused relative; the exclamative What a mess! is a determiner — see the contrast)
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; no plural form, and it is construed as singular unless something in the sentence forces otherwise
entries.refers to: things, events, actions, ideas, amounts, and whole clauses — anything except a person's name. Pointed at a person it asks for the role or category rather than the identity (What is she? — An anesthesiologist.); for the identity, use who. It is open-ended: what assumes no list. For a choice out of a set both speakers can see, use which.
entries.agreement: as subject it takes a singular verb by default — What is in the box?, What happens next? A plural verb appears only when the complement is plainly plural: What are those?, What were the results? Where the answer could go either way, edited American English prefers the plural with a plural complement: What are the remaining options?
entries.pattern: What [verb]? (subject question — no do) · What [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (object question) · What [subject] [verb] [preposition]? (What are you looking at?) · [clause] what [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · [subject] [verb] what? (echo, in place) · What? / What about it? (elliptical)
entries.contrast: what against which is the file's central choice: which selects from a set already on the table, what asks with no set assumed. What did you order? invites any answer; Which did you order? means one of the things in front of us. What against who for a person turns on identity versus role: Who is he? gets my brother-in-law, What is he? gets a structural engineer — and asking What is he? about a person can sound cold, so What does he do? is the ordinary way to put it. Three other whats are not this one: the fused relative (What you said was true = "the thing that"), covered with the fused relatives; the exclamative (What a mess!), which is a determiner; and the determiner what in what color, what time, covered in the determiner dictionary. The test is the same one that runs through both dictionaries: a noun immediately after it makes it a determiner, standing alone makes it a pronoun.
entries.see also: which, who, what (echo), what about, whatever, what (fused relative), what (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to pick one member — or several — out of a set both speakers already have in view.
examples: Which do you want, the aisle or the window?
Which of these chargers is mine?
Which is faster this time of day, driving or the train?
I couldn't tell you which of the twins I spoke to.
Which of you has the parking pass?
Which are we taking, my car or yours?
Which did you end up ordering?
She never said which she had picked.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of witch for most Americans; /hwɪtʃ/ for Southern and older speakers who keep the wh- onset; weak /wətʃ/ in an embedded clause (I forget which one it was)
entries.русский: который, какой из — просит выбрать из закрытого набора, известного обоим собеседникам
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.type: interrogative pronoun (also a relative pronoun)
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; construed as singular or plural according to the answer expected
entries.refers to: things and people alike, but only from a known, bounded set — one that is visible, has just been mentioned, or is listed in the question itself. With people it asks which member of a group (Which of you is Dr. Reyes?), and it never asks for a stranger's identity: ✗Which is she? → Who is she? The set need not be small, only bounded and mutually known (Which state has the longest coastline?).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the expected answer, not with the of-phrase: Which is yours? (one expected) beside Which are yours? (more than one), and Which of these boxes is yours? beside Which of these boxes are ready to ship? With which of us / you / them, a singular verb is the default: Which of us is going to tell him?
entries.pattern: Which [verb]? (subject question — no do) · Which [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Which of [determiner + noun]? · Which [subject] [verb] [preposition]? · [clause] which [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · Which? (elliptical, set understood)
entries.contrast: open set versus closed set is the whole story. What's your favorite movie? leaves the field open to every movie ever made; Which is your favorite? means one of the three on the table. Choosing what when a list has already been given invites an answer from outside the list, and choosing which with no list leaves the hearer hunting for one. Against who for people: who identifies, which selects — Who called? asks for a name, Which of them called? asks you to pick from a group already named. The relative which is a different job (the report, which arrived late) and lives with the relative pronouns — and the famous which/that rule belongs to that entry, not this one: half of it is real (that cannot introduce a nonrestrictive clause) and half is an American editing convention (restrictive which is perfectly grammatical, and a copy editor will still change it to that). The determiner which takes a noun directly (which flight) and lives in the determiner dictionary. Adding of always makes it the pronoun: which flight determiner, which of the flights pronoun.
entries.see also: what, who, which of, whichever, which (relative), which (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks for the identity of a person — the one who did it, or the one it happened to.
examples: Who left the porch light on all night?
Who did you talk to at the bank?
Who's bringing dessert on Thursday?
I still don't know who she voted for.
Who wants to go first?
Who are those people in the driveway?
Who didn't get their parking pass yet?
Who do you think is going to end up paying for it?
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent. No true weak form — as the question word it carries the accent — but it shortens in embedded position, and the contractions are ordinary: who's /huz/, who'd /hud/, who'll /hul/, who're /ˈhuɚ/. Who's is a homophone of whose.
entries.русский: кто — спрашивает об имени, личности человека; форма подлежащего
entries.case: subject — and, in everyday American English, object as well (Who did you call?)
entries.type: interrogative pronoun (also a relative pronoun)
entries.person / number: third person in agreement, whatever person the answer turns out to be; invariant in form, and singular by default no matter how many people the answer names
entries.refers to: people only — including a pet spoken of as a person and a team, band, or company understood as the people in it (Who won?). For a thing use what or which; to pick from a group already named use which of.
entries.agreement: singular by default, even when several people are expected: Who wants coffee?, Who is coming tonight?, Who's got the keys? A plural verb appears only when a plural complement forces it (Who are those men?, Who are the finalists?). Who has no gender, so the pronoun that picks it up afterward is singular they — Who left their coat on the porch?, Whoever called, they didn't leave a message. That is standard American English and not a compromise; see they.
entries.pattern: Who [verb]? (subject question — no do in a neutral question: ✗Who did call?) · Who [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (object question: Who did you call?) · Who [subject] [verb] [preposition]? (stranded: Who did you give it to?) · Who [auxiliary] not [verb]? (negative subject question, where do does appear: Who didn't sign?) · [clause] who [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · Who else, Who all (regional), Says who?
entries.contrast: whom is the object form, and the test is he/him: answer the question and see which fits — Who called? — He called → who; Whom did you see? — I saw him → whom. In real American usage who has taken over the fronted object slot, so Who did you see? is standard rather than an error, and whom survives mainly right after a preposition (to whom, for whom, with whom). Against what for a person: Who is he? asks identity, What is he? asks occupation. Against which: who identifies out of the blue, which selects from a set. And the two do-support facts that trip learners: a positive subject question takes no do (Who called?), but a negative one does (Who didn't get paid?), and emphatic did returns when a denial is being challenged (Somebody called — so who did call?). Who's with an apostrophe is who is / who has, never possessive: see whose. Answering a who question is where case actually shows itself in speech, and the facts are these. The bare answer takes the object form — Who wants coffee? — Me, not ✗I — and It's me is standard English, with It is I now stiff outside the telephone formula This is she. When the answer is built out into a full subject the subject form returns (Who went? — She and I went), and in an object slot the object form returns (Who did they invite? — They invited my wife and me). The hypercorrections are the mirror image of the schoolroom error: ✗between you and I, ✗They invited my wife and I, ✗He gave it to Bob and I — every one of those is an object slot, two of them after a preposition (between, to) and one after a verb (invited), and the object form is what belongs in all three: between you and me, They invited my wife and me, He gave it to Bob and me. The deletion test settles them: drop the other person and read what is left aloud — He gave it to me ✓ against ✗He gave it to I, They invited me ✓ against ✗They invited I, I went ✓ against ✗Me went, which is also what rules out ✗Me and him went. Between is the one place the test needs a second step, because deleting the partner leaves the phrase incomplete; put a plural in instead, and between us shows the case plainly — never ✗between we. Full treatment with me and I.
entries.see also: whom, whose, what, which of, what else, who else, whoever, who (relative), who's (not a possessive pronoun), me, they (singular they)

entries.meaning: Marks the person who is the object of the verb or of a preposition in the question.
examples: Whom did the board finally appoint?
To whom should I address the complaint?
Whom are we meeting at four?
For whom was the second reservation made?
She wouldn't say whom she had consulted before signing.
Whom do you trust with a key to the building?
Whom did they notify first, the family or the press?
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent. It keeps its full vowel almost everywhere, because it is usually being chosen deliberately; the one place it genuinely weakens is inside a fixed prepositional phrase in fast speech, where to whom can flatten to [tə ˈhəm]. The w stays silent even there — there is no /w/ sound in whom at any speed, so ✗[təˈwəm] is not a pronunciation of it.
entries.русский: кого, кому — объектная форма who, при глаголе или предлоге; формальн., книжн.
entries.case: object
entries.type: interrogative pronoun (also a relative pronoun)
entries.person / number: any person, singular or plural; people only, and invariant in form
entries.refers to: human referents only, in an object slot — the object of a verb (Whom did they hire?) or of a preposition (For whom is this?). For things the object form is simply what or which, neither of which marks case.
entries.agreement: none of its own. Being an object, it never controls the verb; the verb agrees with the clause's own subject — Whom did the committee choose? has committee as subject.
entries.pattern: Whom [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · [preposition] whom [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · [clause] whom [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · To whom? / For whom? (elliptical) · the fixed salutation To Whom It May Concern
entries.contrast: the he/him test decides it: if the answer takes him, the question takes whom. Beyond that, be honest about the state of the language. In ordinary American speech and in most published prose, who has replaced whom in fronted object position — Who did you see? is standard American English, not a mistake, and Whom did you see? sounds careful or stiff depending on the room. Where whom is still genuinely required is immediately after a preposition: ✗to who did you speak will be corrected everywhere, while Who did you speak to? is fine because the preposition has been left at the end. The trap now runs the other way: writing whom where the word is the subject of an embedded clause is a hypercorrection and is more common than the error it was meant to prevent — ✗Whom shall I say is calling? (test: he is calling) and ✗the candidate whom we thought would win. Intervening words like we thought and shall I say never change the case.
entries.see also: who, whose, to whom, for whom, with whom, whomever, whom (relative)

entries.meaning: Asks who owns, wrote, made, or is otherwise responsible for the thing in question. ---
examples: Whose is the truck blocking the driveway?
Whose are these sunglasses?
Somebody left a phone on the bench and nobody knows whose it is.
Whose was the idea to leave at four in the morning?
Whose is this — yours or your brother's?
She wouldn't tell me whose it was.
Whose are we taking, since mine is in the shop?
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent, and it is a perfect homophone of who's (= who is / who has). No weak form; as a question word it takes the accent.
entries.русский: чей — спрашивает о владельце, авторе или ответственном за предмет
entries.case: possessive
entries.type: interrogative pronoun (also a relative pronoun; and a determiner in whose coat)
entries.person / number: invariant — it asks about a possessor of any person, number, or gender at once
entries.refers to: possessors. As an interrogative the possessor asked about is almost always human (Whose is this?); the wider power of whose to take inanimate possessors (a building whose roof leaks) belongs to its relative use. What it points at is the owner, never the thing owned.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed, not with whose: Whose is this?, Whose are these?, Whose was the idea? Nothing about whose itself is singular or plural.
entries.pattern: Whose [be] [noun phrase]? (Whose is this jacket?) · Whose [be] [demonstrative]? (Whose are those?) · Whose [be] it? · [clause] whose [subject] [verb] (embedded: I asked whose it was) · Whose? (elliptical)
entries.contrast: whose against who's is the commonest spelling error in this whole class, and the test is expansion: if who is or who has fits, it takes the apostrophe (Who's coming?), and if the sentence is about ownership it does not (Whose is this?). The apostrophe form is never possessive — no possessive pronoun in English has one, which is the same fact behind its/it's and your/you're. Determiner against pronoun is the other line: a noun right after it makes it a determiner (Whose coat is this? — see the determiner dictionary), and standing alone makes it the pronoun (Whose is this coat?, Whose is this?). Note also that whose has no partitive: ✗whose of these does not exist, and the job goes to which of — Which of these is yours?
entries.see also: who, whom, whosever, which of, whose (possessive pronoun), whose (relative), whose (determiner), who's (not a possessive pronoun)

entries.meaning: Asks for the number or the amount, leaving the thing counted or measured to be understood.
examples: How many are coming to the walkthrough on Saturday?
How much is the gray one in the window?
"We'll take the shrimp." "How many?"
How much of the deposit do we get back if we cancel now?
Nobody could tell me how many had already shipped.
How many of you have actually read the lease?
She asked how much it would run us to have the tree taken down.
entries.pronunciation note: standing alone the accent sits on many or much, because the noun that would otherwise carry it has been left out; put a noun back and the accent shifts forward onto how (HOW many PEOPLE came?). How keeps its full vowel everywhere and has no weak form, but the second word reduces when the phrase is unaccented in an embedded clause — I don't know how many are left runs to [haʊ məni], how much of it to [haʊ mətʃ] — and of is the weak /əv/, often bare [ə], so how many of them is [ˈhaʊ ˌmɛni ə ðəm]
entries.русский: сколько — how many о счётных предметах, how much о количестве, мере или цене
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.type: interrogative pronoun — a quantifier standing as the head of its own noun phrase; the same two words in front of a noun are determiners
entries.person / number: third person, invariant in form; how many is plural and how much singular, and the two split the field between them by countability
entries.refers to: a number (how many) or an amount, extent, or price (how much) of something already named or plain from the situation — How many are coming? counts the people under discussion, How much is it? asks a price. What is counted in units takes how many, what is measured takes how much. Neither asks for identity; that is what or which.
entries.agreement: the understood noun controls the verb, not the phrase: How many are left? against How much is left? In the partitive the noun inside the of-phrase decides — How many of the files were deleted? beside How much of the paint was wasted? — and with how many of us / you / them the plural is the normal choice: How many of us are actually going?
entries.pattern: How many [verb]? (subject question — no do: How many showed up?) · How much [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much is [noun phrase]? (the price question) · How many of / How much of [determiner + noun]? · [clause] how many [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · How many? / How much? (elliptical) · never directly in front of a noun in this use — a noun there makes it a determiner
entries.contrast: the noun test settles the part of speech here exactly as it does for what and which: how many chairs has a noun after it and is a determiner (see how many and how much in the determiner dictionary), while How many do we need? stands alone and is the pronoun in this entry. Adding of makes it a pronoun as well — how many of the chairs — and the noun inside the of-phrase keeps its own determiner, so ✗how many of chairs is impossible; that is the same of-rule that governs which of and what of. Countability is where learners actually go wrong: ✗how much people → how many people, ✗how many money → how much money, and a measure word brings the countable form back (how many gallons of gas). Against what, English asks a price with how much and not with what as the subject — ✗What costs the jacket? is a direct translation that never sounds native, though What did it cost? is ordinary. And a third how much is neither pronoun nor determiner but a degree adverb, with no noun anywhere in the sentence: How much do you care?, How much longer? Nothing counted or measured is expected as the answer there.
entries.see also: what, which of, what of, how many (determiner), how much (determiner), how many of, how much of (determiner dictionary)

entries.term: to whom, for whom, with whom
entries.meaning: Fronts the preposition along with its object, producing the formal version of a question about a person.
examples: To whom should I send the signed copy?
For whom is the second ticket?
With whom did you discuss the settlement?
To whom am I speaking, please?
He asked to whom the account had been transferred.
"I need to hand this to somebody." "To whom?"
From whom did the tip actually come?
entries.pronunciation note: the preposition reduces to its weak form (to /tə/, for /fɚ/) and whom takes the accent; in rapid speech to whom flattens to [tə ˈhəm], the one context in which whom really does weaken — the /h/ survives and the w stays silent throughout
entries.русский: кому, для кого, с кем — предлог вынесен вперёд вместе с whom; формальн.
entries.case: object, governed by the preposition
entries.type: interrogative pronoun inside a fronted (pied-piped) prepositional phrase
entries.person / number: any person, singular or plural; invariant, and people only
entries.refers to: human referents only. With a thing, the same frame takes which — to which, for which, with which, in which — and with a thing in ordinary speech the preposition simply goes to the end: What did you open it with?
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb agrees with the subject of the question (For whom were the tickets bought?)
entries.pattern: [preposition] whom [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · [preposition] whom? (elliptical: To whom?) · [clause] [preposition] whom [subject] [verb] (embedded) · the everyday alternative with the preposition stranded: Who [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] [preposition]?
entries.contrast: this is the last position in which whom is genuinely obligatory. When the preposition comes forward with it, only whom is possible; ✗to who, ✗for who, ✗with who are nonstandard for essentially every careful speaker and will be corrected. When the preposition is left at the end, everyday American English uses who: Who did you speak to? Both patterns are correct English and they differ in register, not grammar — the fronted version is formal and can sound stiff in conversation, the stranded version is standard everywhere except the most conservative prose. The one thing to avoid is mixing them. The fossil To Whom It May Concern keeps its capitals as a letter salutation.
entries.see also: whom, who, what for, whom (relative)

entries.meaning: Puts a person or a thing back on the table — either as something being overlooked or as a suggestion.
examples: What about the deposit? Do we get any of it back?
We can take my car. What about the kids' seats?
What about Thursday afternoon for the walkthrough?
I'm fine, thanks. What about you?
"You were an hour late." "What about it?"
What about asking the neighbors before we call the city?
That covers the roof. What about the gutters?
entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps and the words run together, [wʌɾəˈbaʊt]; casual whaddabout
entries.русский: а как же…?, а что насчёт…? — напоминает о забытом или предлагает вариант
entries.case: object of about
entries.type: interrogative pronoun plus preposition, frozen into a frame
entries.person / number: invariant; the following noun phrase can be any person or number
entries.refers to: whatever the following noun phrase names — a person, a thing, a date, a plan — or an -ing clause naming an action (What about calling them first?)
entries.agreement: the elliptical frame is verbless, so nothing agrees: What about the dog? is a complete utterance with no verb in it at all.
entries.pattern: What about [noun phrase]? · What about [-ing clause]? · What about it? · What about you? (turning the question back) · What about [noun phrase] — [tag question]?
entries.contrast: two jobs, told apart by context and intonation. Raising a neglected item: We've booked the flights. — What about the dog? Making a suggestion: What about Thursday? In the second job how about is the more common American choice and it also accepts a full clause (How about we meet Thursday?), which what about resists. The confrontational What about it? is not a request for information but a challenge meaning "so what?" The literary equivalent of the whole frame is what of; the blunt one is so what.
entries.see also: what, what of, so what, what if

entries.meaning: Asks for an exhaustive answer — every person, or everything, that fits.
examples: Who all is coming to the cookout Saturday?
What all did the inspector write up?
I can't even remember what all we ordered.
Who all did you invite besides the Hendersons?
What all is included in the base price?
She told me who all had signed the letter.
Who all was at the courthouse that morning?
entries.pronunciation note: usually run together as one word, [ˈwʌɾɔl], [ˈhuɔl], with all unstressed and hanging on the pronoun like a suffix
entries.русский: что именно (всё), кто именно (все) — диал., юж.-амер.; требует исчерпывающего ответа
entries.case: as the bare pronoun — who all subject or object, whose all does not exist
entries.register: regional — Southern and Midland American English, spoken; entirely standard inside those dialects, absent from formal writing, and unusual in the North and West
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with the exhaustive marker all
entries.person / number: invariant; who all takes people and expects a list, what all takes things and events
entries.refers to: the full membership of a set. Who all is coming? asks for the whole guest list, not for one name; What all did she say? asks for everything that was said.
entries.agreement: singular verb, exactly as with plain who, even though the expected answer is a list: Who all is coming? The plural Who all are coming? occurs but is much less common.
entries.pattern: Who all [verb]? · What all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · [clause] what all [subject] [verb] (embedded: I don't know what all she told him) · also who all's (possessive, spoken)
entries.contrast: the all here is not a quantifier attached to a noun — it is an exhaustiveness marker attached to the question word, and it changes what counts as a complete answer. Plain Who came? can be answered with a single name; Who all came? asks you to name everybody. Speakers outside the region reach for a periphrasis instead — Who came, all told?, Who was there besides Ray?, Everything she said — what was it? — none of which is as economical. Label it accurately: this is a genuine feature of Southern American English rather than an error, but an editor outside the South will delete it, and it does not belong in formal prose. The determiner counterpart takes a noun directly (what all kinds of paperwork) and is covered in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: who, what, what else, who else, what all (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks for what remains after the obvious answers have been given.
examples: What else do we need from the store?
Who else knew about the transfer before Monday?
Who else's car was in the lot at midnight?
What else did the doctor tell you?
I asked him what else had gone missing.
Who else is there to call at this hour?
"You apologized?" "What else could I do?"
entries.pronunciation note: the accent moves onto else, and the t of what flaps into it
entries.русский: что ещё, кто ещё — спрашивает об оставшемся сверх уже названного
entries.case: as the bare pronoun; the possessive is who else's
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with the postposed modifier else
entries.person / number: invariant; who else people, what else things
entries.refers to: the remainder of a set after something has already been accounted for. Both forms presuppose that at least one item is already known, which is why What else do you need? is odd as the first thing you say to someone.
entries.agreement: singular verb: What else is on the list?, Who else is coming? — the same default as bare who and what, no matter how long the remaining list turns out to be.
entries.pattern: What else [verb]? · Who else [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · who else's [noun] (possessive) · What else? (elliptical) · [clause] what else [subject] [verb] (embedded)
entries.contrast: else always follows the pronoun and never precedes it: ✗else what. The possessive is who else's, with the -'s on the end of the whole phrase exactly as in somebody else's — ✗whose else is not English. The object form whom else exists and behaves exactly like whom: formal, and genuinely needed only after a fronted preposition (To whom else did you show it?), where ordinary speech says Who else did you show it to? And note the gap in the paradigm: which else is not used. For a remainder inside a defined set, English switches to a determiner — Which other flight is there?, What other options do we have? What else also has a rhetorical life meaning "obviously": What else could I say?
entries.see also: what, who, what all, who all, somebody else's, what other, which other

entries.meaning: Turns the conversation to something that has been left out, or asks how much of a thing remains.
examples: What of the families still waiting for news?
We have the funding. But what of the timeline?
"You left without telling anyone." "What of it?"
What of the promises made last spring?
And what of the man who signed the order?
What of the original building actually survives?

senses.head: Topic shift (literary)
body: "And what is to be said about X?" — What of the families still waiting? Almost always rhetorical, and almost always in writing or in speech that is being performed.

senses.head: What of it? (fixed)
body: A challenge, equivalent to So what? and just as blunt.

senses.head: Partitive (formal)
body: "What part of" — What of the original manuscript survives? Here a verb follows and agrees with the of-phrase.
examples: What of the families still waiting for news?
We have the funding. But what of the timeline?
"You left without telling anyone." "What of it?"
What of the promises made last spring?
And what of the man who signed the order?
What of the original building actually survives?

entries.pronunciation note: of is the weak /əv/ and often reduces to a single [ə]; the t flaps, giving [ˈwʌɾəv]
entries.русский: а как же…?, что же с…? — книжн., риторический вопрос об упущенном
entries.case: none — the of-phrase is its complement
entries.register: formal, literary, or rhetorical; rare in ordinary conversation
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with an of-phrase
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: a topic that has been set aside — a person, a plan, or a thing already in the discussion — or, in the partitive sense, a portion of something
entries.agreement: the frame is verbless in its main use: What of the others? has no verb to agree with anything. In the partitive sense the verb agrees with the of-phrase: What of the original building survives?
entries.pattern: What of [noun phrase]? (topic shift) · What of it? (fixed challenge) · What of [noun phrase] [verb]? (partitive: What of the estate is left?) · headline and rhetorical use with no verb at all
entries.contrast: it does the same job as what about, one register higher: What of the survivors? is what a novelist writes, What about the survivors? is what a person says out loud. What of it? is fixed, confrontational, and means exactly so what. Keep it apart from the partitive which of: which of the plans asks you to pick one from a known list, what of the plans asks what is to be said about them. The determiner dictionary treats the same string from the determiner side under what of.
entries.see also: what about, so what, which of, what, what of (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks for the reason — the archaic why, fused out of where and for.
examples: "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" (Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet — asking why he must be a Montague, not where he is)
"Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?" (Job 21:7, King James Version)
"Wherefore criest thou unto me?" (Exodus 14:15)
"Friend, wherefore art thou come?" (Matthew 26:50)
The clerk asked wherefore the writ had issued, and nobody in the room could say. (embedded — costume English, statement order)
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that the Court enter judgment in her favor. (the living American use — a consequence marker meaning "therefore," not a question)
She wanted all the whys and wherefores before she would sign anything. (the fixed plural noun, likewise not a question)
entries.pronunciation note: both syllables keep their full vowels when it opens a question and takes the accent; in the surviving legal and conjunctive use it is unaccented and the second syllable weakens to [-fɚ], [ˈwɛrfɚ], exactly the reduction therefore undergoes. Plain /w/ for most Americans, /hw-/ for speakers who keep the older onset
entries.русский: почему, отчего, по какой причине — устар.; архаичный предок why и what for
entries.case: none
entries.register: archaic — an American meets it in Shakespeare, in the King James Bible and hymn texts that quote it, and, still alive and daily, in the closing paragraph of legal pleadings
entries.type: interrogative pro-form — where- (here meaning "what") fused with the preposition for, the same construction as whereof and whereby; in modern grammatical description an interrogative adverb rather than a pronoun, since it fills an adverbial slot and can be neither subject nor object
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: a reason or purpose — "for what reason", "to what end". Never a place, and never a person or a thing: what it stands in for is an adverbial, which is why it sits at the edge of this dictionary rather than in the middle of it. For a thing the parallel fossil is whereof ("of which"), and for a person there is no where- form at all.
entries.agreement: none of its own. As an adjunct it never controls the verb; in the archaic question the verb agrees with its own subject and inverts around it — Wherefore art thou Romeo?, Wherefore do the wicked live?
entries.pattern: Wherefore [verb] [subject]? (archaic direct question, with inversion and no do-support) · [clause] wherefore [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · the living consequence marker, which is not a question at all: [clause]; wherefore, [clause] · WHEREFORE, [party] prays … (the prayer for relief that closes an American complaint) · the fixed plural noun the whys and wherefores
entries.contrast: the misreading first, because it is nearly universal: Juliet's Wherefore art thou Romeo? asks why he has to be a Montague, not where he is standing, and the balcony makes the wrong reading almost irresistible. What replaced the word is why in general and what for where the question is specifically about purpose — What did you do that for? is the living descendant of the construction, preposition stranded instead of fused. Be honest about the classification: unlike whether, which genuinely was a pronoun meaning "which of two" before it died, wherefore never filled a noun-phrase slot at all; it is catalogued here because the wh- question words belong together and because its where- half is the same pro-form that shows up in whereof, wherein, and whereby — all of which are catalogued with the archaic and dialectal pronouns. Its two living jobs are not interrogative and are covered elsewhere: the conjunctive adverb meaning "therefore," which takes a semicolon before it and a comma after, and the legal WHEREFORE clause, both in the conjunction dictionary. Add the fixed noun the whys and wherefores, and that is the whole of the word's modern life; nothing here belongs in a question an American would actually ask.
entries.see also: what for, what, whether, whereof, whereby, whence, wherefore (conjunctive adverb), wherefore (formal and archaic), why

entries.meaning: Asks which one of two — the archaic ancestor of a job which now does alone.
examples: "Whether of them twain did the will of his father?" (Matthew 21:31, King James Version)
"Whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold?" (Matthew 23:17)
"Whether of the twain will ye that I release unto you?" (Matthew 27:21)
"Shew whether of these two thou hast chosen." (Acts 1:24)
"Whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and walk?" (Matthew 9:5)
Whether of the two roads is the shorter, the river road or the turnpike?
She asked whether the check had cleared. (The living use — a conjunction introducing an embedded question, not a pronoun standing in for the answer.)
entries.pronunciation note: a perfect homophone of weather for most Americans; speakers who keep the older wh- onset say /ˈhwɛðɚ/, and theirs is the one accent in which the two words are told apart by sound. As a question word it takes the accent and keeps its full vowel; in the living conjunction use it is unaccented and weakens to [wəðɚ] (I don't know whether it matters), and in fast speech the medial /ð/ can drop altogether, [ˈwɛɚ]
entries.русский: который из двух — устар. и вымершее местоимение; ныне эту роль целиком взяло which
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.register: archaic, out of ordinary use since the seventeenth century; an American meets it today in the King James Bible and in older literature quoting it, and essentially nowhere else
entries.type: interrogative pronoun — archaic; the living word spelled this way is a subordinating conjunction
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; construed as singular, since it picks one out of two
entries.refers to: one of exactly two things or people already named — the two-member counterpart of which. The restriction is built into the word: whether carries the same comparative -ther that sits in either, neither, and other, and Old English hwæþer meant "which of two" where hwilc asked out of many. For three or more, older English used which — which is what English now uses for both.
entries.agreement: singular verb, whichever of the two turns out to be the answer: Whether is greater, the gold, or the temple? (Matthew 23:17). With a partitive of-phrase it stayed singular as well — Whether of them twain did the will of his father? (Matthew 21:31).
entries.pattern: Whether [singular verb] [option] or [option]? (direct question — archaic) · Whether of [the two / them / them twain] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (partitive — archaic) · the living patterns belong to the conjunction, not the pronoun: [clause] whether [clause] (She asked whether the check had cleared) · whether or not · whether to [verb] · whether … or …
entries.contrast: one spelling, two words, and only the dead one is a pronoun. As a pronoun whether meant "which of two", and it is gone: no American says ✗Whether do you want, the soup or the salad? — that sentence is Which do you want …? today, because which absorbed the job and English gave up the two-versus-many distinction entirely, the same way it gave up hwilc against hwæþer. What survives is the conjunction, which introduces an embedded yes/no or alternative question (I asked whether he was coming) and is covered in the conjunction dictionary; it fills no noun-phrase slot, takes no case, and can never itself be the answer to anything, which is exactly what keeps it out of this dictionary. In that job it is if that has to be kept apart from it: only whether survives after a preposition (the question of whether to appeal), only whether goes straight in front of to (whether to sell), and only whether keeps the alternative reading unambiguous — Tell me if you're going can be read as "in the event that you go", while Tell me whether you're going cannot. Older English also put whether directly in front of a noun, and a word in that position is a determiner rather than a pronoun; that use died with the pronoun, and the living interrogative determiners are in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: which, which of, what, whether (conjunction), whether or not

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to pick one or more members out of a set that the question itself names.
examples: Which of these chargers is yours?
Which of us is going to tell her?
Which of the two routes is faster this time of day?
Which of the applicants did the committee actually interview?
I couldn't say which of them called first.
Which of you has a car seat in the back?
Which of the boxes are ready to go out today?
entries.pronunciation note: of weakens to /əv/ and in fast speech to [ə], so which of us runs to [wɪtʃ əˈvʌs], or with the /v/ dropped altogether, [wɪtʃ əˈʌs]
entries.русский: который из, кто из — просит выбрать из группы, названной в самом вопросе
entries.case: none
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with a partitive of-phrase
entries.person / number: invariant; singular or plural according to the answer expected
entries.refers to: members of a set spelled out in the of-phrase — people and things equally: which of the applicants, which of these keys, which of us
entries.agreement: the verb follows the expected answer, not the plural noun after of: Which of these keys opens the shed? when one is expected, Which of these keys open the shed? when more than one might. With which of us / you / them the default is singular: Which of us is going to tell him?
entries.pattern: Which of [the / these / my + plural noun]? · Which of [us / you / them]? · Which of [the two]? · Which of [noun phrase] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · never before a bare plural: ✗which of applicants
entries.contrast: the of-test is what makes this a pronoun rather than a determiner: which flight takes a noun directly and is a determiner, which of the flights stands on its own and is a pronoun. Because the noun inside the of-phrase keeps its own determiner, of must be followed by the, a demonstrative, a possessive, a number word, or a pronoun. Against who for people, which of them selects from a group already named while who asks for an identity out of nowhere. And note that whose has no partitive at all — ✗whose of these is yours → Which of these is yours?
entries.see also: which, who of, whom of, whose, whichever, which of (determiner dictionary)

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to pick a member out of a set in view, with the number of the answer stated by the pronoun itself.
examples: Which one do you want, the blue or the gray?
Which ones are ready to go out today?
Which one of you has the parking pass?
I couldn't tell which one she was pointing at.
"Hand me the smaller wrench." "Which one?"
Which one is your brother — the one in the ball cap?
She never said which ones she had already paid for.
entries.pronunciation note: the two words run together into one piece, [wɪtʃˈwʌn]. The accent lands on one only when the choice itself is being pressed (Which one, the blue or the gray?); in the ordinary question it stays on which and one drops to the weak [wən] — Which one do you want? is [ˈwɪtʃ wən …], and which ones weakens the same way to [wənz]. Plain /w/ for most Americans, /hwɪtʃ/ for Southern and older speakers who keep the wh- onset
entries.русский: который именно, которые именно — разговорная развёрнутая форма which
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.register: neutral; this is the ordinary spoken form, and bare which is the clipped, slightly more formal one
entries.type: interrogative pronoun phrase — the interrogative determiner which sitting on the prop-word one, the two of them filling a single noun-phrase slot
entries.person / number: third person; which one singular and which ones plural, and the form chosen announces the number of the expected answer before the verb arrives
entries.refers to: members of a known, bounded set — things, animals, and people alike, exactly as bare which does. With people it picks a member out of a group in view (Which one is your brother?) and never asks for a stranger's identity: ✗Which one is she? → Who is she?
entries.agreement: the verb follows the form chosen: Which one is yours? against Which ones are yours? With a partitive of-phrase the singular form keeps a singular verb however plural the noun after of is — Which one of these keys opens the shed?, Which one of us is going to tell him? That is the practical advantage over bare which, where Which is yours? leaves the number to be guessed at.
entries.pattern: Which one [verb]? (subject question — no do) · Which one [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Which one of [determiner + plural noun]? · Which ones [verb]? · [clause] which one [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · Which one? / Which ones? (elliptical) · which one … the other one (contrastive pair)
entries.contrast: against bare which the meaning is identical and the weight is not: one spells the number out and is what Americans actually say, while bare Which do you want? is a shade more clipped and more formal. Against which of, the set is named in the sentence (which of these chargers) instead of left understood, and the two combine freely: which one of these chargers. Against who for people, which one selects from a set in view where who asks for an identity out of nowhere. What is a determiner here is worth stating plainly: inside the phrase, which is a determiner sitting on the noun-like one, and it is the whole phrase — not which alone — that does the pronoun's work, which is the same analysis given to this one / that one and the reason this entry sits in the pronoun dictionary while which flight sits in the determiner dictionary. Put a real noun in the slot and the whole thing is determiner plus noun; keep the prop-word one and it is this entry. One frequent worry does not apply here: the American objection to these ones (see these ones / those ones) is an objection to a demonstrative propped on ones, and no editor blinks at which ones. And there is no what counterpart — ✗What one do you want? is not American idiom, because an open-set question has no set to count members out of; it is simply What do you want?
entries.see also: which, which of, what, who, whichever, this one / that one, these ones / those ones, one, ones, which (determiner)

entries.meaning: Picks out members of a named group of people, usually in a rhetorical question.
examples: Who of us has not sat through a meeting like that?
Who of the original crew is still with the company?
Whom of the three finalists would you trust with the account?
He asked who of the tenants had actually complained.
Who of you would have said no to an offer like that?
Who of them can honestly claim to be surprised?
entries.pronunciation note: of weak /əv/
entries.русский: кто из — книжн., риторическое; о членах названной группы людей
entries.case: who of subject, whom of object
entries.register: literary and rhetorical; marginal in ordinary American English
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with a partitive of-phrase
entries.person / number: invariant; people only
entries.refers to: members of a group of people named in the of-phrase
entries.agreement: singular verb: Who of us has not made that mistake?
entries.pattern: Who of [us / you / them] [verb]? · Who of [the + plural noun] [verb]? · [preposition] whom of [noun phrase]? (rare) · almost always in a rhetorical question expecting the answer "none of us"
entries.contrast: the ordinary partitive for people is which of — Which of us is going? — and that is what to use in plain prose. Who of survives mainly in the rhetorical "who among us" register, and even there who among us is the more idiomatic frame. Whom of is rarer still and reads as hypercorrect unless a preposition actually governs it; if a preposition does not, use who of or rewrite. Nothing is ungrammatical here, but the whole entry is a stylistic choice rather than a working part of the language.
entries.see also: which of, who, whom, what of

entries.meaning: Mocks the formality of whom by piling on endings that never existed. ---
examples: Whomst has the aux cord?
To whomst do I owe the pleasure?
"Whomst?" she typed back, three seconds after his text.
Whomst've among us has not hit reply-all by accident?
Whomst did they put in charge of the spreadsheet, exactly?
The group chat spent an hour escalating from whom to whomst'd've.
He signed off "regards, whomstve," and nobody in the thread acknowledged it.
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent, exactly as in whom; the final cluster is awkward enough that an intrusive [p] often turns up, [humpst]. There is no weak form — the word exists in order to be noticed, so it always carries the accent — and the longer forms scan as written: whomst'd /humstəd/ HOOMST-ud, whomst'd've /ˈhumstədəv/ HOOMST-ud-uv
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — шуточное интернет-передразнивание чопорного whom
entries.case: object in shape; in practice it is written into subject slots as freely as object ones, because the joke does not track case
entries.register: nonstandard — internet slang, humorous, current online among younger American writers since the later 2010s and out of place in any writing that is not itself joking
entries.type: jocular pseudo-archaic variant of whom — an internet coinage, not a historical English form
entries.person / number: any person, singular or plural; people only, and invariant
entries.refers to: human referents, exactly as whom does. The extra letters carry no meaning whatever: what they add is a performance of over-formality, usually aimed at the writer's own pretension rather than at anyone else's.
entries.agreement: none of its own in the object use. Where the joke drops it into subject position — which real whom does not allow — the verb is singular by default: Whomst has the aux cord?
entries.pattern: Whomst [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Whomst [verb]? (subject use, ungrammatical for real whom and part of the joke) · [preposition] whomst? · bare Whomst? / Whomst've? as an exclamation of mock astonishment · the escalating ladder whom → whomst → whomst'd → whomst'd've, each rung longer than the last
entries.variants: whomst've, whomstve, whomst'd, whomst'd've — the apostrophes are optional and inconsistent, since nothing is actually being contracted — plus open-ended nonce chains built by piling on more clitics (whomst'd'st, and strings written purely for the joke of their length); whomst've is the commonest of the extended spellings, and whomstve the commonest way of writing it without punctuation
entries.contrast: there is no historical whomst, and saying so plainly is the whole entry. The -st is borrowed by ear from two real things — the -st of whilst, amongst, and amidst, and the old second-person verb ending of thou dost and thou canst — but it never attached to whom in Old, Middle, or Early Modern English, and no standard dictionary records the word. The genuinely old extended forms are whomso and whomsoever, and neither is related to this. What the joke is about is whom itself: in American English whom already reads as a status marker, the word people reach for when they want to sound careful and the word they most often get wrong (the hypercorrect ✗Whom shall I say is calling?), so bolting a fake ending onto it mocks that impulse — commonly the writer's own. Practically, there is no context in which it is the right choice for a real question: where a true object form is wanted the word is whom, obligatory only after a fronted preposition, and everywhere else ordinary American English says who.
entries.see also: whom, who, whomever, whomso, whomsoever, whom (relative)

entries.meaning: Asks what with astonishment, bewilderment, or exasperation built in.
examples: Whatever do you mean by that?
Whatever possessed you to sign it without reading it?
Whatever is the matter with the dog tonight?
Whatever happened to the couple who lived upstairs?
Whatever will they think of next?
Whatever did she say to make him leave like that?
entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps, giving [wʌˈɾɛvɚ], and casual speech reduces the first syllable to [wə-]; in the emphatic question a heavy accent lands on -EV-
entries.русский: что же это такое?! — what с изумлением; в амер. англ. книжн., устар., «на британский лад»
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object
entries.register: literary, dated, or British-flavored in American English
entries.type: emphatic interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; construed as singular
entries.refers to: things, events, and actions, exactly as bare what does — the -ever adds astonishment, not meaning. It never refers to a person's identity.
entries.agreement: singular verb, as with what: Whatever is going on?, Whatever has become of them?
entries.pattern: Whatever [verb]? (subject question — no do) · Whatever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · two-word variant What ever …? · American colloquial equivalents: What on earth …?, What in the world …?, What the heck …?
entries.contrast: three different whatevers, and only the first is in this file. (a) Emphatic interrogative — Whatever do you mean? — the entry here. (b) Fused relative — Take whatever you need, meaning "anything that", covered with the fused relatives; it appears in statements, not questions. (c) The dismissive interjection — Whatever., meaning "I don't care" — an interjection, not a pronoun, and rude in most company. Spelling follows the split: two words for the emphatic question, one word for the relative. The determiner whatever takes a noun directly (whatever excuse he gives) and lives in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: what, whoever, whichever, what (echo), whatever (fused relative), whatever (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks which with disbelief that any of the available options could be the answer.
examples: Whichever of the two could he possibly have meant?
Whichever will she choose, after complaining about all of them?
Whichever did they end up sending, in the end?
Whichever of these routes could be the scenic one?
Whichever would you pick, if you had to pick one today?
Whichever of the applicants is he thinking of, after that interview?
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on -EV-; /hwɪtʃˈɛvɚ/ for speakers who keep the wh- onset
entries.русский: который же из них?! — which с недоверием к самим вариантам; редк., книжн.
entries.case: none
entries.register: rare as a question word — literary at best; ordinary and frequent only in its fused-relative use
entries.type: emphatic interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person, invariant; singular or plural by the answer expected
entries.refers to: members of a known, bounded set, like bare which; the -ever adds astonishment that any member of the set could be the answer
entries.agreement: follows the expected answer, singular by default: Whichever is he going to pick?
entries.pattern: Whichever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Whichever of [noun phrase] …? · two-word variant Which ever …? · the ordinary American alternative: Which on earth …? or simply Which …?
entries.contrast: be honest about the frequency: as a genuine question word whichever is close to unattested in modern American speech, and a speaker wanting the emphatic version of which just says Which one on earth …? or leans on intonation. Overwhelmingly, whichever is a fused relative (Take whichever you want = "any one that") or a determiner (whichever route is faster), and neither of those is a question — see the fused relatives and the determiner dictionary. If what you are writing is a question and the -ever form sounds strained, that is because it is; drop back to which.
entries.see also: which, which of, whatever, whichever (fused relative), whichever (determiner)

entries.meaning: Asks who with astonishment that any person at all fits the description.
examples: Whoever told you that?
Whoever could be calling at this hour?
Whoever would want to drive that far twice a week?
Whoever let the dog in the house?
Whoever thought putting the printer upstairs was a good idea?
Whoever does she think she is, rewriting the whole contract?
entries.pronunciation note: the two words run together with no break, [huˈwɛvɚ]; the accent on -EV-
entries.русский: кто же это?! — who с изумлением; разг., единственная живая -ever-форма вопроса
entries.case: subject (and object in everyday use, exactly as with who)
entries.register: informal to neutral — the one -ever question form still fully alive in American speech
entries.type: emphatic interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person in agreement; invariant, and singular by default
entries.refers to: people only, like bare who; the -ever adds disbelief that any person could be the answer
entries.agreement: singular verb: Whoever is calling at this hour?, Whoever wants a job like that?
entries.pattern: Whoever [verb]? (subject question — no do) · Whoever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · two-word variant Who ever …? · American colloquial equivalents: Who on earth …?, Who in the world …?
entries.contrast: against the fused relative whoever (Whoever finishes first should start the next batch), which is a statement subject meaning "the person who" and belongs with the fused relatives. One string, two grammars, and the question mark tells them apart: Whoever told you that? is a question about a person's identity, while Whoever told you that was wrong is a statement about whoever it was. Case: the emphatic question uses whoever even in object position in ordinary speech (Whoever did they hire?), and whomever there is a formality most Americans skip. The classic error is the mirror image — ✗give it to whomever wants it, where the word is the subject of its own clause and must be whoever.
entries.see also: who, whomever, whatever, whosever, whoever (fused relative)

entries.meaning: Asks whom with astonishment — the object-case, formal counterpart of whoever.
examples: Whomever did they appoint to run the committee?
To whomever could that letter have been addressed?
Whomever did the trustees have in mind for the position?
For whomever was such an enormous house built?
Whomever did he imagine he was fooling?
Whomever could they have been protecting all those years?
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on -EV-
entries.русский: кого же?! — объектная пара к whoever; очень редк., подчёркнуто формальн.
entries.case: object
entries.register: very rare and highly formal as a question word; the ordinary spoken form in an object question is whoever
entries.type: emphatic interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: any person, singular or plural; invariant, and people only
entries.refers to: human referents only, in an object slot
entries.agreement: none of its own — as an object it never controls the verb: Whomever did the committee appoint?
entries.pattern: Whomever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · [preposition] whomever [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · two-word variant Whom ever …?
entries.contrast: everything true of whom is true here in a sharper form. As a question word whomever is vanishingly rare and, outside a fronted preposition, it reads as hypercorrect; even careful American writers use Whoever did they hire? or simply Who did they hire? Where the word earns its keep is the fused relative in object position — Give it to whomever you choose — and even there the test matters: the case is decided by the job the word does inside its own clause, so give it to whoever wants it is correct because whoever is the subject of wants, and ✗whomever wants it is the single most common -ever error in edited American prose. When in doubt, substitute him: if him fits the slot inside the clause, whomever is right.
entries.see also: whom, whoever, to whom, for whom, with whom, whomever (fused relative)

entries.meaning: Asks — or, more often, concedes without asking — who the owner is, when the owner is unknown.
examples: Whosever can this umbrella be, left here all week?
Whosever it is, they should have claimed it by now.
The wallet on the counter — whosever it is, leave it where it is.
Whosever these are, they don't belong in the hallway.
Whosever it turns out to be, the boat still has to be moved.
"Whosever is this?" she asked, holding up a single glove.
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent and the accent falls on -EV-; the spelling variants whoseever and the two-word whose ever are also found
entries.русский: чей же?; чей бы он ни был — редк., книжн., юр.; о неизвестном владельце
entries.case: possessive
entries.type: emphatic interrogative possessive pronoun (and a fused-relative possessive)
entries.person / number: invariant; asks about a possessor of any person, number, or gender
entries.refers to: possessors, effectively always human in this use
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed, never with whosever: Whosever these are, they don't belong here.
entries.pattern: Whosever [be] [noun phrase]? (question — archaic) · Whosever [pronoun] [be], … (fused relative: Whosever it is, they should claim it) · the determiner use takes a noun directly: whosever coat
entries.contrast: it is the -ever form of whose, and both of its uses are rare. As a question (Whosever can this be?) it is essentially archaic; an American says Whose on earth is this? or, far more often, just Whose is this? As a fused relative (Whosever it is should come and get it) it still turns up in writing, though many writers prefer Whoever's or rewrite the sentence entirely. One spelling point: the -ever attaches to the already-possessive whose, so there is no apostrophe anywhere — ✗whose'ever, ✗whosever's. The determiner counterpart is in the determiner dictionary.
entries.see also: whose, whoever, whosever (possessive pronoun), whosever (fused relative), whosever (determiner)

entries.term: what on earth, who on earth
entries.meaning: Asks the same question the bare pronoun asks, with astonishment or exasperation attached. ---
examples: What on earth is that supposed to mean?
Who on earth would drive out there in this weather?
What on earth did you do to the printer?
Who on earth told him about the party?
What in the world are we going to tell the inspector?
"What the heck is that noise?" he said, getting up.
She looked at the bill and thought, what on earth.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent moves off the question word and onto the intensifier, and on earth links into one piece, [ɑˈnɚθ]; the variants scan the same way, with the reduced to its weak /ðə/ and the accent on the intensifier — the heck /ðə ˈhɛk/ thuh-HEK, the hell /ðə ˈhɛl/ thuh-HEL, in the world /ɪn ðə ˈwɚld/ in-thuh-WERLD, in God's name /ɪn ˈɡɑdz ˌneɪm/ in-GODZ-name
entries.русский: что же (кто же), чёрт возьми — усиление вопроса; вариант the hell — груб.
entries.case: as the bare pronoun — who on earth subject or object, whom on earth the formal object form, whose on earth the possessive
entries.register: on earth and in the world neutral to informal; the heck and the devil mild; the hell profane, and out of place in writing that is not quoting speech
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with an emphatic adjunct
entries.person / number: invariant; who on earth takes people, what on earth things and events
entries.refers to: exactly what the bare pronoun refers to — the adjunct adds astonishment, exasperation, or impatience and changes nothing else. Who on earth called at midnight? asks the same question as Who called at midnight?, with feeling attached.
entries.agreement: singular verb, the same default as bare who and what: Who on earth is knocking?, What on earth was that noise? The adjunct is invisible to agreement.
entries.pattern: What on earth [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Who on earth [verb]? (subject question — no do) · the adjunct sits immediately after the question word and never floats: ✗What do you on earth mean? · also Which on earth …? and Whose on earth …? (both marginal) · bare What on earth? / What the heck? (elliptical)
entries.variants: what in the world, who in the world, and marginally which in the world (neutral to informal, and the commonest American alternative to on earth) · what the heck, who the heck, what the dickens, what the devil (mild, and the printable ones) · what the hell, who the hell (profane), and what the fuck, who the fuck (obscene) — speech and quoted dialogue only · what in God's name, who in God's name, what in heaven's name (grave rather than casual) · what in blazes, what in tarnation (dated and rural; an American now meets tarnation mainly in cartoons and old Westerns) · every one of them sits immediately after the question word and changes nothing but the register
entries.contrast: this is the living American replacement for the -ever forms. Where an older novel or a British speaker has Whatever do you mean?, an American says What on earth do you mean? or What the heck do you mean? The family sorts by register and nothing else: on earth and in the world go anywhere, the heck and the devil are mild, in God's name is the emphatic-formal one, and the hell is profanity — accurate to label, easy to misjudge in print. Two spin-offs are not questions at all: what the hell as a shrug of consent (Oh, what the hell — order the big one), and the bare What the …? left unfinished as an exclamation of surprise. None of it belongs in edited prose except inside dialogue.
entries.see also: what, who, whatever, whoever, what (echo), so what

entries.meaning: Announces news by pretending to ask for a guess.
examples: Guess what — they approved the loan.
Guess who I ran into at the airport.
"Who's there?" "Guess who!"
Guess what happened on the way home.
Guess who's coming to dinner tomorrow night.
Guess what she said when I told her the price.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the question word, and the whole phrase usually falls rather than rises, because no answer is really wanted
entries.русский: угадай что, угадай кто — разг., шутливое предисловие к новости
entries.case: the wh- clause is the object of guess, and the wh- word itself takes whatever case its own clause gives it — subject in Guess who's coming, object in Guess who I saw
entries.type: imperative verb with an embedded interrogative pronoun, frozen as an opener
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: a piece of news the speaker is about to deliver (guess what), or a person (guess who)
entries.agreement: no verb of its own beyond the imperative. When a clause follows, the embedded verb agrees normally and is singular by default: Guess who's coming to dinner.
entries.pattern: Guess what! · Guess who! · Guess what [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order: Guess what she said) · Guess who's [verb-ing]? · Guess who. (as an answer, at a door or on the phone)
entries.contrast: it is not a real question — it is an attention-getter announcing news, and the expected response is What?, not a guess. Punctuation follows function: Guess what! I got the job. takes an exclamation point or a period far more often than a question mark. Guess who has a second life as an answer: knocking on a door and saying Guess who! Word order inside a following clause stays statement order — Guess who I saw, never ✗Guess who did I see.
entries.see also: what, who, who's who, what (echo)

entries.meaning: Asks what to do at a point where the plan has run out.
examples: The car won't start. Now what?
Okay, the form is signed. What now?
Now what — we can't even get in without a badge.
"The flight's canceled." "Now what?"
What now, do we just wait for them to call us back?
Every time the phone rings I think, now what.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent falls on the second word in both, and exasperation flattens the contour rather than raising it
entries.русский: и что теперь? — разг., когда план исчерпан или случилась новая помеха
entries.case: none
entries.type: elliptical interrogative
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the next step, or the next thing to go wrong
entries.agreement: verbless — there is nothing in either phrase for a verb to agree with
entries.pattern: Now what? · What now? · So now what? · expanded: Now what do we do? / What do we do now?
entries.contrast: Now what? usually carries exasperation — one thing has already gone wrong and here comes another. What now? can carry the same, but it is also a neutral request for the next step, which Now what? rarely is. Both are ellipses of What do we do now? Keep them apart from what next, what then: now what is about the present impasse, what next about the sequence still to come.
entries.see also: what next, what then, what, so what, what if

entries.meaning: Closes a question by leaving every other possibility unnamed.
examples: Are we ordering, or what?
Is that a sunset or what?
So is he coming to the meeting or what?
Do you want the job or what?
"Well? Are you going to tell me or what?"
Was that the strangest interview you have ever sat through or what?
entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to [ɚ] and the two run together as [ɚˈwʌt]; the accent is on what, and the tone rises sharply at the end
entries.русский: или как?, или что? — разг., закрывает вопрос, не называя прочих возможностей
entries.case: none
entries.type: interrogative pronoun closing an elliptical alternative question
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the unnamed alternatives — what stands in for "any other possibility", left deliberately unspecified because the speaker does not care to list them
entries.agreement: none of its own; the clause in front carries all of it (Are we going or what?, Is he coming or what?)
entries.pattern: [yes/no question] or what? · Is that [noun phrase] or what? (rhetorical admiration) · Are you going to [verb] or what? (impatience) · a main-clause tag only — it embeds badly (?I asked whether we were going or what)
entries.contrast: one shape, two feelings that are nearly opposite. Impatience: Are we leaving or what? presses for a decision and can be rude. Rhetorical admiration: Is that a view or what? is not asking anything — it demands agreement, and the expected answer is yes. Both are ellipses of a genuine alternative question (…or what are we doing?), and the what is a real pronoun standing for the option nobody bothered to name. Keep it apart from a spelled-out alternative question (Are we driving or flying?), where the second option is given and what has no work to do. Spoken only: in writing it belongs in dialogue.
entries.see also: what, what (echo), so what, now what, what now

entries.meaning: Challenges a claim by demanding to know who is behind it.
examples: "You can't park there." "Says who?"
Who says we have to leave at six?
"That's not how it works." "Says who?" "Says the manual."
Who says you can't teach an old dog new tricks?
"You're too old to start over." "Says who?"
Who says it has to cost that much?
entries.pronunciation note: says is /sɛz/, never /seɪz/
entries.русский: кто это сказал?, а кто сказал? — разг., вызов: требует назвать источник утверждения
entries.case: subject — who is the subject of says in both orders
entries.type: elliptical interrogative, frozen
entries.person / number: invariant; third-person singular verb
entries.refers to: the person whose authority is being challenged
entries.agreement: third-person singular says, fixed: ✗who say. The past-tense Who said? and Said who? exist but are separate, milder questions asking who actually spoke.
entries.pattern: Says who? · Who says? · Who says [clause]? (Who says we have to be there at eight?) · the stock reply Says me.
entries.contrast: the inverted Says who? and the plain Who says? mean the same thing — "on whose authority?" — and both are challenges rather than requests for a name. The stock reply Says me puts an object form where a subject belongs, and it is a deliberate idiom rather than an error to be corrected; it still has no place in writing, and the "corrected" ✗Say I is not English at all. Who says also takes a full clause, where it becomes a rhetorical denial: Who says it has to cost that much? means "it doesn't."
entries.see also: who, who cares, who knows, so what

entries.meaning: Asks for a repetition, usually with disbelief attached.
examples: "I sold the truck this morning." "Say what?"
Say what? You drove all the way to Reno for a sandwich?
"They want the whole thing by Friday." "Say what now?"
He looked up from the bill and said, "Say what?"
"Your cousin is moving in with us." "Say what?" "For a month, maybe two."
"Rent's going up two hundred dollars." "Say what?!"
"She quit on the spot." "Say what? She'd been there eleven years."
entries.pronunciation note: a hard rise on what, which carries the accent and is often drawn out, [ˈwʌːt]; the two words run together and say takes the weak [sə] in fast speech, giving [səˈwʌt]. What has no weak form here — it is the questioned word, so it can never reduce to [wət] the way it does in I know what I want
entries.русский: чего?, что-что? — разг., просьба повторить с недоверием; из афроамериканского англ.
entries.case: object — what is the object of say, and it does not front
entries.register: informal and spoken; it began in African American English and spread into general informal American speech over the second half of the twentieth century, and an editor will cut it from anything that is not dialogue
entries.type: frozen imperative with the interrogative pronoun left in place — an echo question in shape
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the piece of what was just said that the hearer missed or cannot believe — the same thing the wh- word picks out in any other echo question
entries.agreement: none — the imperative has no subject to agree with, and nothing inside the phrase inflects: ✗said what? and ✗says what? are not this idiom, and there is no past-tense version of it at all
entries.pattern: Say what? · Say what now? · drawn out for comic disbelief, Say whaaat? · it stands alone as a whole turn and takes no continuation: ✗Say what did he tell you? · and it does not embed — ✗I asked him say what (say I asked him to say it again)
entries.contrast: it belongs to the family of ways to ask for a repetition, and register is what sorts them: Sorry?, Excuse me?, and I'm sorry, what? are the polite ones, Huh? and Come again? the casual neutral ones, bare What? the blunt one, and Say what? the one that carries disbelief with it — far more often "I can't believe you just said that" than a genuine request to hear it again. Its history is worth stating plainly rather than hinting at: it is African American English in origin and is now general American slang, used across the board in speech and marked as casual rather than as dialect. Two things it is not. The ordinary imperative Say what you mean has a full clause after it and is not this idiom. And You don't say registers surprise at news without asking for anything, where Say what? asks. Structurally it is an echo question — the wh- word stays where it is, there is no do-support, and the tone rises hard.
entries.see also: what (echo), what, guess what, guess who, what's up, so what

entries.meaning: Refuses to accept that what was just said matters.
examples: "He's twenty years older than she is." "So what?"
So what if we're the last ones there?
She read the memo twice and thought, so what?
"You'll be the only one in a suit." "So what?"
So what — nobody is going to check the receipts.
Every slide has to answer the so-what.
entries.pronunciation note: a heavy accent on what and a falling tone — it is punctuated as a question but does not sound like one
entries.русский: ну и что? — разг., резко; отрицает важность только что сказанного
entries.case: none
entries.register: informal; blunt, and rude in the wrong company
entries.type: elliptical interrogative used as a dismissal
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the point just made, which the speaker refuses to treat as important
entries.agreement: verbless
entries.pattern: So what? · So what if [clause]? · So what? as a stand-alone reply · noun use: the so-what, the so-what test
entries.contrast: a rhetorical question with falling intonation: it takes a question mark by convention and expects no answer. Milder ways to make the same move are Does it matter?, What about it?, and a bare And?; the formal and equally confrontational version is What of it? The noun use — every slide has to answer the so-what — is business jargon for the point of a piece of information, and it is hyphenated.
entries.see also: what, what about, what of, who cares, who knows

entries.meaning: Repeats back the part of what was just said that the hearer missed or cannot believe.
examples: "I sold the truck." "You did what?"
She's marrying who?
He said what to the officer?
You paid what for a used dishwasher?
"I quit this morning." "You what?"
Wait — you told who about the offer?
The company is doing what with our data?
entries.pronunciation note: the echoed wh- word carries the nuclear accent and the whole utterance rises hard at the end; it is often lengthened, [wʌːt]
entries.русский: что?, как ты сказал? — переспрос-эхо: недослышал или не может поверить
entries.case: whatever the slot requires — but see the note below on who
entries.type: interrogative pronoun in an echo question
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the piece of the previous utterance that the hearer missed, or cannot believe
entries.agreement: none of its own — the clause keeps the verb it already had, unchanged: She said what?, never ✗She did say what?
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] what? (in place, no fronting, no do) · [subject] did what? · [subject] [verb] who? · You what? · bare What? · the same rise on any other question word: He's marrying who?
entries.contrast: an echo question breaks the two rules the rest of this file runs on. The wh- word does not move to the front, and there is no do-support: You did what? is an echo, while What did you do? is an ordinary question asking for information the speaker never had. Case relaxes too — in an echo, the object slot takes who even in careful speech (You called who?), and whom there sounds arch. A bare What? as a request for repetition is blunt in American English; Sorry?, Excuse me?, Come again? and I'm sorry, what? are the polite versions and Huh? the casual one. Say what? is a further casual variant — it began in African American English and is now general informal American speech, spoken only, and an editor will cut it from anything but dialogue. An echo can even target a wh- question itself: Who did what?
entries.see also: what, who, say what, whatever, guess what, guess who, Reported questions

entries.meaning: Asks what the purpose of something is.
examples: "I'll need your license." "What for?"
