What did you tell her that for?
What's this bracket for?
What are we all standing in line for?
She asked what the second key was for.
He came home at two in the morning and his mother gave him what for.
"Bring your passport." "What for? It's a domestic flight."
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on for, which keeps its full vowel because it is stranded at the end; the t of what flaps, [wʌɾ ˈfɔr]
entries.русский: зачем, для чего, с какой целью — вопрос о цели
entries.case: object of for
entries.type: interrogative pronoun with a stranded preposition
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: a purpose — the goal an action was aimed at
entries.agreement: the elliptical What for? is verbless; in the full pattern the clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement (What is this bracket for?)
entries.pattern: What for? (elliptical) · What [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] [object] for? (What did you do that for?) · What's it for? · [clause] what [subject] [verb] for (embedded) · the idiom give someone what for
entries.contrast: What for? and Why? both ask for a reason, but what for asks specifically about purpose, while why covers cause as well. A pipe bursting has a cause and no purpose, so Why did the pipe burst? works while What did the pipe burst for? is odd — not ungrammatical, just asking after a purpose that a burst pipe does not have. In this idiom the preposition stays at the end and is not fronted: What did you buy that for? is ordinary, and the pied-piped ?For what did you buy that? is stilted rather than wrong — it is grammatical, which is why it gets a question mark here and not a cross, but nobody says it — though For what purpose …? is fine in formal writing. The frozen idiom give someone what for means to scold them sharply, and there what for is a noun phrase, not a question.
entries.see also: what, what about, to whom, for whom, with whom, what if

entries.meaning: Asks for an explanation of something that does not make sense.
examples: You've been quiet all night. What gives?
The store is closed on a Tuesday — what gives?
What gives with the new parking rules?
So what gives? Are we going or not?
I asked him what gives and he just shrugged.
Three emails and no answer. What gives?
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on gives
entries.русский: в чём дело?, что происходит? — разг., амер. сленг середины XX в.
entries.case: what is the subject
entries.register: informal; mid-century American slang that survives comfortably in speech
entries.type: fixed interrogative expression
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: an unexplained situation — something that is not adding up
entries.agreement: gives is frozen in the third-person singular present. There is no ✗what gave or ✗what is giving in this idiom; to put it in the past you have to rewrite (I asked what was going on).
entries.pattern: What gives? · So what gives? · What gives with [noun phrase]? · embedded: I asked him what gives
entries.contrast: it means "what is going on?" or "what's the problem?", and it is an idiom rather than a live use of give — no ordinary sense of the verb is involved. The neutral equivalents are What's going on?, What's the deal?, and What happened? It is casual and slightly dated; nobody will misunderstand it, but it will read as a period detail in writing.
entries.see also: what, now what, what now, so what, what's what

entries.meaning: Closes a list by gesturing at everything else of the same kind.
examples: Bring a sleeping bag, a flashlight, what have you.
The garage is full of paint cans, old tile, and what have you.
They'll want pay stubs, bank statements, or what have you.
He does the taxes, the payroll, what have you — the whole back office.
We can meet at the office, a coffee shop, what have you.
She kept every card, letter, and ticket stub, and what have you, in one shoebox.
entries.pronunciation note: in running speech it flattens to [wʌɾəvjə] — the t flaps, have reduces to [əv], and you to its weak form [jə]; it is said quickly and low, as the tail end of a list
entries.русский: и тому подобное, и всё такое прочее — завершает перечисление, не называя остального
entries.case: what is the object of have inside the frozen clause
entries.register: neutral to informal; ordinary in speech and in relaxed writing
entries.type: frozen interrogative clause used as a noun phrase
entries.person / number: invariant — the you is frozen and never changes person: ✗what have they, ✗what has he
entries.refers to: the open remainder of a list — "and other things of that kind", with the speaker declining to name them
entries.agreement: frozen solid. No tense, person, or number moves inside it: ✗what had you, ✗what have we. When the list is in the past, the surrounding sentence carries the tense — the drawer was full of receipts, coupons, and what have you.
entries.pattern: [list], and what have you · [list], or what have you · [list], what have you (bare) · it closes a list and never opens one
entries.contrast: it does the job of and so on, and so forth, et cetera, and the more casual and whatnot or and all that, and register is what separates them: et cetera is the formal one, and so on the neutral written one, what have you and whatnot the conversational ones. Grammatically it is a fossil — a question in shape with no question left in it — which is why the you cannot change and why it never takes a question mark. Keep it out of technical, contractual, or legal prose, where an open-ended list needs including but not limited to rather than a shrug.
entries.see also: whatnot, what, what's what, what gives, what (fused relative)

entries.meaning: Asks what would follow if some supposed situation came true.
examples: What if the flight is delayed again?
What if we just told them the truth?
What if she says no?
What if I had taken the other job?
He kept asking what if the tests came back positive.
What if we met halfway, somewhere around Bakersfield?
The whole proposal is a pile of what-ifs.
entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps and links into the vowel, [wʌˈɾɪf]
entries.русский: а что, если… — вводит предположение и спрашивает о его последствиях
entries.case: subject of the missing main clause
entries.type: interrogative pronoun heading an elliptical conditional question
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the consequences of a hypothetical situation — what stands for the whole unstated outcome
entries.agreement: the if-clause carries its own agreement and the main clause is simply left out: What if it rains? is What (will happen) if it rains?
entries.pattern: What if [present clause]? (live possibility) · What if [past clause]? (remote: What if we missed it?) · What if [past perfect clause]? (counterfactual: What if she hadn't called?) · noun use: a what-if, the what-ifs
entries.contrast: the ellipsis is in the main clause, not the if-clause, so the if-clause keeps ordinary statement order and ordinary conditional tense marking. Three degrees of remoteness sit on the same frame: What if it rains? treats rain as a live possibility, What if it rained? holds it further off, What if it had rained? is counterfactual and about the past. It doubles as a suggestion — What if we left at six instead? — where how about would do the same work. As a noun it is hyphenated: we ran through all the what-ifs.
entries.see also: what, what about, what next, what then, now what, what now

entries.meaning: Asks what comes next in a series, or what follows from a supposition.
examples: We've painted the hallway. What next?
Suppose they refuse to sign. What then?
First the flood, then the furnace — what next!
If we sell the house, what then?
She asked me what next and I had no answer for her.
And what then, when the money runs out in March?
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the second word
entries.русский: что дальше?, а потом что? — о следующем шаге или о следствии предположения
entries.case: none
entries.type: elliptical interrogative
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the next item in a sequence (what next), or the consequence of something already supposed (what then)
entries.agreement: verbless in the elliptical form
entries.pattern: What next? · And what then? · What then [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · the exclamatory What next! · embedded: she asked what next
entries.contrast: What next? asks what comes after in a series, and in its exclamatory use — first the roof, now the furnace, what next! — it registers dismay at an accumulation rather than asking anything, which is why it takes an exclamation point there. What then? asks about a consequence and needs a supposition in front of it to lean on: Suppose the bank says no. What then? Against now what, what now, which is about the present impasse rather than the sequence ahead.
entries.see also: now what, what now, what if, what, so what

entries.meaning: Closes a list by waving at everything else of the same kind.
examples: Bring chips, soda, and whatnot — whatever you'd want on the boat.
The shed is full of rakes, hoses, and whatnot.
She handles scheduling, payroll, whatnot — the whole front office.
They'll want pay stubs, tax returns, or whatnot.
There were flyers, coupons, and whatnot jammed into the screen door.
He collects stamps, coins, and whatnot, and none of it is worth much.
entries.pronunciation note: one stress, on the first syllable; the t of what is unreleased or glottalized before the n, [ˈwʌʔnɑt], and the whole word is said fast and low at the tail of a list
entries.русский: и всё такое, и прочее — разг., завершает перечисление взмахом руки
entries.case: none — the what inside it is frozen and neither takes nor assigns case
entries.register: informal to neutral; ordinary in speech and in relaxed writing
entries.type: frozen interrogative clause (what not) fused into a noun phrase
entries.person / number: invariant; neither singular nor plural, and it never takes a verb of its own
entries.refers to: the open remainder of a list — "and other things of that kind" — the same job what have you does, with the speaker declining to name the rest. It closes lists of things, not of people: rakes, hoses, and whatnot is ordinary, and a list of people takes and so on or and the rest instead.
entries.agreement: none — the phrase is a fossil with no verb inside it, so nothing in it agrees with anything. The surrounding sentence carries all the tense and number: the drawer was full of stamps, rubber bands, and whatnot.
entries.pattern: [list], and whatnot · [list], or whatnot · [list], whatnot (bare) · it closes a list and never opens one · the unrelated count noun a whatnot (a small shelved stand)
entries.contrast: it stands in the same slot as what have you, and so on, and so forth, et cetera, and and all that, and register is the only thing that separates them: et cetera is the formal one, and so on the neutral written one, whatnot and what have you the conversational ones, with whatnot a shade the more casual of the pair. Two mechanical points. It is written solid, as one word in this use: and whatnot. The two-word and what not is the older spelling and still surfaces, but American dictionaries and copy editors have settled on the solid form, and an editor will close it up. And there is no question left in it at all: it takes no question mark, and it cannot be fronted, inverted, or embedded as a real question — ✗Whatnot did you buy? The homograph a whatnot, a nineteenth-century piece of furniture with several small shelves, is an ordinary count noun with a plural (two whatnots) and is not a pronoun at all. Keep the list-closer out of contracts and specifications, where an open-ended list needs including but not limited to rather than a shrug.
entries.see also: what have you, what, what's what, what (fused relative)

entries.meaning: Refuses a question by challenging the asker's right to ask it.
examples: "How much did you pay for it?" "What's it to you?"
"You're not going to the reunion?" "What's it to you?"
He asked where I'd been all afternoon, and I said, what's it to you.
"Is he still living out there by the lake?" "What's it to ya?"
What's it to you who I have lunch with on a Tuesday?
She has a way of asking what's it to you without saying a word.
"Just curious how the interview went." "What's it to you?" "Nothing. Forget I asked."
entries.pronunciation note: the accent lands on you, which keeps its full vowel because it is the point of the challenge; to is the weak /tə/ and the t of what's it flaps, so the whole phrase runs to [wʌtsɪɾəˈju]. Let the accent fall back onto what instead and the weak forms take over the end, giving the casual what's it to ya [ˈwʌtsɪɾəjə]
entries.русский: тебе-то какое дело? — разг., грубовато; отказ отвечать через встречный вызов
entries.case: none — what is a predicate complement here, neither subject nor object
entries.register: informal and spoken; confrontational, and rude between people who are not close
entries.type: fixed interrogative expression — what as the complement of be
entries.person / number: invariant in practice; what's it to him and what's it to them occur, but they read as reports of the same challenge rather than as fresh ones
entries.refers to: the stake or the concern the hearer has in the matter — and the expected answer is "none". It never asks for information; what here stands for an interest the speaker is denying the hearer has.
entries.agreement: the contracted is is fixed and singular: ✗what are it to you. The past What was it to you? is grammatical but rarely said — the idiom lives in the present tense, and the older What is that to thee? (John 21:22, King James Version) is the same frame with an archaic pronoun in it.
entries.pattern: What's it to you? (a whole turn on its own) · What's it to ya? (casual spelling) · And what's it to you? · What's it to you [wh- clause]? (What's it to you who I have lunch with?) · the older What's that to you? · a that-clause after it is stiff — for that, say What business is it of yours that …
entries.contrast: it is a challenge, not a question: it refuses the question just asked instead of answering it, and the expected reply is a retreat. The family sorts by heat — Why do you ask? is neutral, What business is it of yours? is sharper and can be said in full sentences, What's it to you? is blunter still and belongs to speech, and Mind your own business drops the question shape altogether. Against its neighbors in this section: So what? dismisses the importance of what was said, What about it? dares the hearer to make something of it, and what's it to you attacks the hearer's standing to have asked at all. The older wording What's that to you? is the King James phrasing and now reads as scriptural or archaic; what's it to ya is the same sentence with the weak forms written out, and belongs only in dialogue.
entries.see also: so what, what about, who's to say, says who, who says, what (echo)

entries.meaning: Asks what is new or what is wrong — or greets, and asks nothing.
examples: "What's up?" "Not much — you?"
What's up with the front door? It sticks now.
Hey, what's up — you look upset.
She stopped by to see what's up with the schedule change.
I asked him what was up and he said the server had been down all morning.
Nobody would tell me what was up with the delay.
What's up, you two? Need a hand with that?
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ and /s/ form a cluster that resyllabifies onto up, [wʌˈtsʌp]; casual speech drops the /t/ altogether, giving whassup [wəˈsʌp] and, reduced further, 'sup [sʌp]
entries.русский: что нового?, что случилось? — разг.; а также приветствие «привет, как дела?»
entries.case: what is the subject
entries.register: informal; ordinary in speech everywhere in American English, and whassup / 'sup more casual still
entries.type: fixed interrogative expression — what as subject of be
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: whatever is new, happening, or wrong — and, in the greeting use, nothing at all
entries.agreement: the contracted is is singular and fixed; the past what was up is ordinary (I asked what was up), but ✗what are up is not English
entries.pattern: What's up? (greeting) · What's up? (real question) · What's up with [noun phrase]? · [clause] what's / what was up (embedded, statement order) · the stock reply Not much.
entries.contrast: two jobs sharing one string. As a greeting it is phatic — the expected answer is Not much or Not a lot, and answering it in detail misreads it. As a real question it asks what is new or what is wrong, and it is usually marked either by a with-phrase (What's up with the printer?) or by heavy stress and a worried face. Its neighbors sort by assumption: What's going on? is neutral, What gives? asks for an explanation and is dated, What's the matter? assumes something is already wrong. The spellings whassup and 'sup are speech transcribed and belong in dialogue only. Not to be confused with the adjective up in something's up ("something is going on"), which is a different construction with no question in it.
entries.see also: what, what gives, now what, what now, what's what

entries.meaning: Names the real facts of a situation, considered as a thing you can know or explain.
examples: Give her a week and she'll know what's what.
Somebody needs to sit that contractor down and tell him what's what.
Until the audit is finished, nobody knows what's what.
He talks a good game, but he doesn't really know what's what.
It took me a month on the job to figure out what's what.
She explained what's what about the lease in about four minutes.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the second what
entries.русский: что к чему — истинное положение дел как нечто, что можно знать и объяснить
entries.case: none — the first what is the subject, the second the complement
entries.type: frozen embedded interrogative clause, used as a noun phrase
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the essential facts of a situation — which things are which, and what actually matters
entries.agreement: the is inside the contraction is fixed and singular; the past-tense what was what is ordinary (nobody could tell what was what), but a plural is not: ✗what were what
entries.pattern: know what's what · tell [someone] what's what · figure out what's what · past tense what was what
entries.contrast: an embedded question that has hardened into an idiom for "the true state of affairs." Know what's what means to be well informed and hard to fool; tell someone what's what means to set them straight, usually sharply. The people-version is who's who. It is not used as a direct question in American English — ?What's what? as an opener is not idiomatic (odd, not ungrammatical), though What's up? and What's going on? are perfectly ordinary.
entries.see also: who's who, what, what gives, Reported questions

entries.meaning: Names the problem of telling apart the members of a set you can label but not identify.
examples: The twins were in matching jackets and nobody could tell which is which.
Label the cables now or you'll never know which is which.
Both files are named "final" — good luck figuring out which is which.
She had two sets of keys and no idea which was which.
The plans look identical until you check the dates to see which is which.
I know one of them is the primary account. I just can't tell you which is which.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the second which, the is unstressed to [ɪz] and often reduced to [z] after the first word in fast speech
entries.русский: который из них который, где какой — задача различить похожие предметы
entries.case: none — the first which is the subject, the second the complement, and which has one form for both
entries.type: frozen embedded interrogative clause, used as a noun phrase
entries.person / number: invariant; the set involved always has two or more members, but the clause itself stays singular
entries.refers to: the identities of the members of a known set — which of the things in front of you is which of the ones you already have names for
entries.agreement: singular verb, however many items are in the set: which is which in the present, which was which in the past. ✗which are which is not used, and the singular holds even past two (I can never tell which is which among the three of them).
entries.pattern: tell which is which · know which is which · figure out which is which · past tense which was which · almost always after a verb of knowing or telling, and usually negated
entries.contrast: the third member of the set with what's what and who's who, and the one that stays closest to a live question. It presupposes a bounded set of look-alikes, exactly as bare which does — who's who sorts people, what's what covers the state of affairs in general, and which is which tells apart two or more things you can label but not identify. It is not used as a bare direct question: ?Which is which? on its own is odd rather than ungrammatical, where Which one is mine? would be said. And unlike who's who it has no noun use — there is no ✗a which is which of.
entries.see also: what's what, who's who, which, which of

entries.meaning: Dismisses a point as unimportant, or concedes that the answer is unknown.
examples: "The label says organic." "Who cares?"
Who cares if it rains — we're going anyway.
Who knows how long the permit will take.
"Is he coming back?" "Who knows."
He has, who knows, maybe two hundred of them out in the garage.
Who cares what the neighbors think about the fence?
Who knows what would have happened if we had left an hour earlier.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the verb, and the tone falls — neither is really asking
entries.русский: кому какое дело — пренебрежение; кто знает — признание, что ответа не знает никто
entries.case: who is the subject
entries.register: informal; who cares is dismissive and can be rude, who knows is neither
entries.type: rhetorical interrogative, frozen
entries.person / number: invariant; third-person singular verb
entries.refers to: nobody in particular — the implied answer is "nobody" in both
entries.agreement: third-person singular, fixed: who cares, who knows, never ✗who care. In the past it inflects normally (who knew, which has its own idiomatic life meaning "who would have guessed").
entries.pattern: Who cares? · Who cares if / whether [clause]? · Who knows? · Who knows [wh- clause] (Who knows what he'll say) · parenthetical who knows (It'll take, who knows, another year)
entries.contrast: both are rhetorical questions whose answer is "nobody", but the force is different. Who cares? dismisses the importance of what was just said and is often rude; the softer moves are Does it matter? and So what?, which is blunter still. Who knows? concedes ignorance and offends nobody, and it can float inside a sentence as a parenthetical hedge meaning "possibly" (he's in Denver, or Boise, who knows). When either takes a following clause, that clause keeps statement word order: Who knows what she paid for it?, never ✗who knows what did she pay.
entries.see also: who, says who, who says, so what, Reported questions

entries.meaning: Concedes that nobody can know the answer — or that nobody has the standing to judge.
examples: "Would the surgery have helped?" "Who's to say?"
Who's to say what the market will look like in five years?
Maybe he'd have quit anyway. Who's to say.
Who's to say she was wrong to take the money and go?
Who's to say which of the two of them started it?
It might have turned out the same either way — who's to say.
Who's to say what counts as a fair price for a house on that road?
entries.pronunciation note: the w is silent, to is the weak /tə/ and often just [ɾə] after the /z/, and the accent falls on say; the tone falls rather than rises, because nothing is really being asked. Who's is /huz/ and a homophone of whose
entries.русский: кто знает?, кому судить? — никто не может знать или не вправе выносить приговор
entries.case: subject
entries.register: neutral to informal; at home in speech and in relaxed writing alike
entries.type: rhetorical interrogative, frozen — who as subject of the be to construction
entries.person / number: invariant; third-person singular is, contracted to 's in nearly every use
entries.refers to: nobody in particular — the implied answer is "no one", either because no one can know or because no one has the standing to judge
entries.agreement: third-person singular is, fixed: ✗who are to say. The past who was to say is ordinary in narrative (who was to say she was wrong?), and the modal paraphrases who can say and who could say work the same way; ✗who's saying and ✗who's to said are not this idiom.
entries.pattern: Who's to say? (stand-alone) · Who's to say [that-clause]? (Who's to say he's wrong?) · Who's to say [wh- clause]? (Who's to say what would have happened?) · written with a period when the falling tone is being kept: But who's to say. · past who was to say · the following clause keeps statement order
entries.contrast: two shades, both rhetorical, and the be to construction is what separates them. Nobody can know: Who's to say what would have happened if we'd left earlier? — the same concession who knows makes, a degree more considered and a degree more formal. Nobody has the standing to judge: Who's to say which of them is right? — here be to is doing its "be in a position to" work, and the sentence is about authority rather than about knowledge, which is the line between this and who knows. Against says who, who says: that one challenges an authority that has actually been invoked, while who's to say denies that any authority exists. Two mechanical points. A clause after it keeps statement word order, the rule for every embedded question — Who's to say what she meant?, never ✗who's to say what did she mean. And the spelling is who's, the contraction of who is; ✗whose to say is a misspelling, and the test is at whose.
entries.see also: who cares, who knows, says who, who says, who, whose, what's it to you, Reported questions

entries.meaning: Names the question of which person is which, or a roster of the people who matter in a field.
examples: With the twins in matching coats, nobody could tell who's who.
It took me a month to learn who's who in the department.
The reception was a who's who of state politics.
Print name tags so people know who's who.
By the third chapter I had lost track of who's who.
He can tell you who's who on that committee and who actually decides anything.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent on the second who
entries.русский: кто есть кто — различение людей в группе; тж. «список видных лиц» (a who's who of)
entries.case: who in both slots — the first is the subject of the contracted is, the second its complement, and ✗who's whom is not English
entries.type: frozen embedded interrogative clause, used as a noun phrase
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: the identities of the people in a group — which person is which
entries.agreement: the verb is always singular, however many people are involved: who's who in the present, who was who in the past, never ✗who are who
entries.pattern: tell who's who · know who's who · figure out who's who · past tense who was who · the noun a who's who of [field]
entries.contrast: the people-version of what's what, and it carries two senses worth keeping apart. As a clause it means "which person is which" — with the masks on, you couldn't tell who's who. As a noun, a who's who of is a roster of the notable people in a field — the guest list was a who's who of Nashville songwriting. Spelling: who's here is who is and takes the apostrophe, so ✗whose who is simply a misspelling; see whose for the test.
entries.see also: what's what, who, whose, guess what, guess who
